items.title: Trump Reportedly Tells Aides Iran Action Resumes After the Midterms
items.idea: Trump confirmed Saturday he rejected Iran's proposed seven-day ceasefire framework and, per WSJ reporting the newsletter corroborates independently, told aides he expects military action against Iran could resume after the November midterms. This lands the same week as Wednesday's PCE print and Friday's payrolls (~100k consensus, 4.2% unemployment), with the 10-year already above 5% and the Fed hiking for the first time in three years.
items.angle: The market is treating this as background noise, not a scheduled escalation. A Hormuz risk explicitly timed to reopen post-midterms, stacked on a week where strong data is now bad news for yields, is three catalysts sharing one narrow landing strip.
items.tweetA: Trump reportedly told aides he expects Iran action to resume after the midterms — that's not a random flare-up, that's a scheduled reopening of the Hormuz risk. The market is pricing this as background noise into a week with PCE, payrolls, and a 10-year already above 5%.
items.tweetB: Wall Street wants payrolls soft enough to cool Fed hike odds but not soft enough to spook growth — the classic Goldilocks ask. Except Goldilocks usually didn't have a president telegraphing a post-midterms military timeline on the commodity that sets the inflation print she's trying to thread.

charts.desc: No inline charts — text analysis of the oil/Fed/breadth backdrop for the coming week.

items.title: The 10-Year Real Yield Just Crossed the Line That Broke 1994, 2000 and 2007
items.idea: The 10-year real yield is now 2.60%, about 100bps above both R* (1.65%) and long-run potential growth. The last three times real yields overtook growth — 1994, 2000, 2007 — each ended in a shock (rate, growth, credit respectively), but every single time the 10-year then fell 240-370bps within 24 months. The catch: debt/GDP was 47% in 1994 versus roughly 100% today.
items.angle: If the pattern holds, real yields this stretched are a leading indicator of their own reversal via recession or crisis, not a stable new regime — the open question is what breaks this time given twice the leverage.
items.tweetA: Every time real yields have overtaken potential growth — 1994, 2000, 2007 — a shock followed, then the 10-year fell 240-370bps in 24 months. We're there again at 2.60% real. The difference: debt/GDP is ~100% now, not 47%. Same trigger, twice the leverage.
items.tweetB: What breaks first when real yields run 100bps above growth for months? History says something always does. The bond market corrected the imbalance itself in 1994, 2000 and 2007. The question this time isn't whether it corrects — it's what gets carried out on the way there.

charts.desc: CHART WORTH SAVING — the author's own words: 'if I could keep only one chart on my desk, it would be this one.' 10Y real yield vs R* and potential growth, with the three historical crossings marked.

items.title: S&P Dispersion Just Hit 2.5x the Dot-Com Peak — With the Index Near Highs
items.idea: Goldman's data (via Macro Mornings) shows the share of S&P 500 stocks moving against the index just hit 44% on a 3-month basis — versus an 18% peak at the height of the dot-com bubble, roughly 2.5x. The top 10 stocks now weigh 40% of the index versus 27% in March 2000. In 2000 itself, small value gained 22.8% while large growth lost 22.4% over the same 12 months — a 45-point gap.
items.angle: If AI leadership wobbles, this data says the other 490 stocks have both further to fall and more room to rotate into — the same setup that preceded 2000's small-value/large-growth reversal.
items.tweetA: Everyone's watching the S&P near record highs. Meanwhile the 3-month dispersion measure — how many stocks are moving against the index — just hit 44%, 2.5x the dot-com peak. The index is calm. The other 490 stocks are not.
items.tweetB: 2000: small value +22.8%, large growth -22.4% in the same 12 months. Today's top 10 weigh 40% of the S&P vs 27% at the 2000 peak. If history repeats when concentration breaks, the trade isn't shorting the index — it's owning what got left behind.

charts.desc: Chart inside — Goldman's 3-month/1-year stock-dispersion-from-index measure plotted against the 2000 dot-com peak, plus a top-10 index-weight chart.

items.title: The Market Is Now the Hawk Against the Fed — History Says That's Worse for Stocks
items.idea: The Fed's dot plot sees 4.125% through 2026-27; fed funds futures price 4.26%/4.80%/4.91%/5.18% through 2029 — a gap that widens to roughly 155bps by 2029. In prior market-vs-Fed standoffs, whoever was proven wrong dictated returns: when the market was the hawk and right (1994, 2022), equities went flat or negative; when the Fed was the hawk and wrong (2018 dots vs 2019 cuts), the S&P gained 28.9%.
items.angle: Right now the market is the hawk, which historically has been the worse setup for equities than a hawkish-but-wrong Fed — every strong data print becomes a headwind, not a relief.
items.tweetA: Fed dots say 4.125% through 2027. Futures say 5.18% by 2029 — a 155bp gap. History's rule: when the market is the hawk and right (1994, 2022), stocks go flat or negative. When the Fed is the hawk and wrong (2018→2019), stocks rally 29%. Guess which regime we're in now.
items.tweetB: As long as fed funds futures sit 100+bps above the dots, every strong jobs or CPI print lands as a hawkish surprise — not because growth is bad, but because the market already priced Fed stubbornness. That's a structurally worse setup for risk assets than 2019's dovish surprise.

charts.desc: Chart inside — Fed dot plot vs fed funds futures curve through 2029, plus the four historical market-vs-Fed standoffs.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Goldman Sachs (Ben Snider)
items.title: Goldman's 8,700 S&P Target Is an Earnings Call, Not a Multiple Call — And the Earnings Are Leveraged to Four CFOs
items.idea: Goldman's 8,700 target (from 7,764) assumes the forward P/E stays flat at 19x — all the upside is earnings growth. Almost half of 2026 S&P EPS growth comes from AI investment spending flowing through chip, hardware, industrial and utility earnings. Hyperscaler capex is on track for $800B this year (+94% YoY), with Goldman modeling $1.2T in 2027 and $1.4T in 2028 — and a $250B swing in either direction would move S&P earnings growth by roughly 6 percentage points. Memory producer gross margins are running near 80%, more than double their historical average.
items.angle: Goldman's own numbers show the index's earnings engine is now a leveraged bet on a handful of hyperscaler capex budgets, not organic demand — which turns the 'AI bubble' debate into a capex-forecasting exercise rather than a valuation exercise.
items.tweetA: Goldman's math: a $250B swing in hyperscaler capex moves S&P 500 earnings growth 6 percentage points either way. That's not a company forecasting its own earnings anymore — that's the index's earnings being set by four CFOs' capex budgets.
items.tweetB: Memory producer gross margins just hit ~80%, double their historical average, and Goldman says that's propping up 'extraordinary' semiconductor earnings growth. When margin expansion this extreme fades — and Goldman itself says it will — where does S&P EPS growth come from instead?

charts.desc: Charts inside — Goldman's EPS growth decomposition by driver and forward P/E history vs the 10-year average.

items.title: ServiceNow's Bear Case (AI Kills Seats) May Have the Mechanism Backwards
items.idea: ServiceNow's revenue per customer nearly doubled from ~$700k (2020) to ~$1.5M (2025), and it now has 658 customers paying over $5M a year with a 98% renewal rate. Its AI products crossed $1B in annual contract value in under three years — faster than most standalone AI startups — because its CMDB and Workflow Data Fabric give AI agents the only map of who-owns-what across a company's tech stack. The stock trades at $137, about 40% below its high, on Street fears that AI-driven productivity compresses per-seat licensing.
items.angle: The bear case assumes AI kills per-seat SaaS pricing; the bull case is that ServiceNow becomes the orchestration layer every enterprise AI agent has to plug into. City of Raleigh already cut IT help desk costs 66% using NOW's AI agents without the company losing that customer's spend.
items.tweetA: $NOW is down 40% from highs because Wall Street thinks AI kills per-seat pricing. But AI agents need a map of who-owns-what to act on anything — and ServiceNow's CMDB is that map. Raleigh already cut IT costs 66% with it. The bear case may have the mechanism backwards.
items.tweetB: ServiceNow's revenue per customer went from $700k to $1.5M in five years, mostly before its AI products existed at scale. If AI ACV crossed $1B in under three years without visibly cannibalizing seats yet, 'seat erosion' looks like a 2028 risk being priced as a 2026 problem.

charts.desc: Charts inside — revenue-per-customer growth trend and the author's NOW DCF/valuation model.

items.title: Intel's Comeback Chip Ties a Three-Year-Old TSMC Node on Density — And Still Outsources Its Own Flagship GPU
items.idea: SemiAnalysis's physical teardown of Panther Lake found Intel 18A's compute logic density matches TSMC's N3E node — but trails TSMC N3P, N2, and Samsung SF2. Panther Lake is the first commercial chip with backside power delivery (PowerVia) and Intel's first gate-all-around transistors (RibbonFET, four stacked nanosheets), assembled via Foveros-S packaging — yet its larger 12-core GPU tile is fabbed on TSMC N3E, not Intel silicon.
items.angle: Intel is manufacturing-competitive in absolute terms again, but the density gap to the nodes that matter for AI (N2, SF2) means 'Intel Foundry catches up' is a 2027+ story — and the company still outsources its own flagship GPU tile to its biggest rival.
items.tweetA: Intel's newest chip — the one meant to prove its manufacturing comeback — uses TSMC silicon for its high-end GPU tile. 18A ties TSMC's three-year-old N3E node on density. It doesn't touch N3P, N2 or Samsung SF2. 'Shipped silicon' and 'competitive silicon' aren't the same claim.
items.tweetB: PowerVia moves power delivery to the backside of the wafer, freeing frontside routing for signal — that's the real story in Panther Lake, not the CPU cores, which are incremental. Whoever nails backside power at scale first gets a real density edge in 2-3 years. Intel just proved it can ship it, not that it can lead with it.

charts.desc: 10+ TEM/EDS cross-section images of the PowerVia backside-via stack and RibbonFET nanosheet gates — a genuine visual teardown, worth opening directly.

items.source: AI Agents Weekly / Elvis Saravia, citing Anthropic
items.title: Claude Opus 5.5 Matches a Flagship Model's Coding Score at 40% Lower Cost
items.idea: Anthropic's Opus 5.5 performs near Claude Fable 5.1 on most tasks at roughly 40% lower cost, scoring 66.4% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 (vs 55.8% for Fable 5.1 and 57.9% for GPT-6 Astra) and an 81.8% on OSWorld 2.0. Pricing dropped to $4/$20 per million input/output tokens with cache reads at $0.20. Anthropic also reports its strongest automated safety-audit result yet, with Opus 5.5 attempting to circumvent boundaries about 85% less often than Opus 5.
items.angle: The frontier price/performance curve keeps compressing faster than raw compute costs fall — that's disinflationary for every AI-app-layer business's unit economics and bullish for adoption curves that were previously cost-gated.
items.tweetA: Opus 5.5 matches a flagship model's coding performance at 40% lower cost, months later. If frontier intelligence keeps getting this much cheaper this fast, every 'AI is too expensive to deploy at scale' objection has a shelf life measured in quarters, not years.
items.tweetB: Anthropic also reports an 85% drop in guardrail-circumvention attempts in Opus 5.5 versus Opus 5. Capability and alignment are usually framed as a tradeoff. This release argues they can compound together — worth watching whether that holds as models get more agentic.

charts.desc: Charts inside — Terminal-Bench, OSWorld and GDPval-AA benchmark comparison bars across Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra.

items.source: AI Agents Weekly / Elvis Saravia, citing OpenAI
items.title: GPT-6 Sol Beats Opus 5's Best Score at 9% of the Cost Per Task
items.idea: OpenAI's GPT-6 Sol scores 33.2% on AutomationBench — a 47-tool, end-to-end workflow benchmark — at $0.27 per task, beating Claude Opus 5 at max effort (26.9%) for about 9% of the cost per task. GPT-6 Luna undercuts further, priced at $0.10/$0.50 per million input/output tokens, and OpenAI says prompt caching now gets a 90% discount by default with GitHub reporting over 50% fewer prompt tokens needing fresh processing.
items.angle: This is the clearest evidence yet that the model price war has shifted from raw benchmark leadership to cost-per-completed-task leadership — the metric that actually determines enterprise agent economics, not the leaderboard.
items.tweetA: GPT-6 Sol beats Claude Opus 5's best score on a 47-tool business workflow benchmark at 9% of the cost per task. The AI competition isn't 'who's smartest' anymore — it's 'who's cheapest per completed task.' That's a different company to bet on than the benchmark leaderboard suggests.
items.tweetB: $0.10 per million input tokens for GPT-6 Luna. Two years ago that would have looked like a typo. The cost curve on 'good enough for routing and classification' tasks has collapsed faster than most enterprise AI budget models assumed — worth checking if your own cost forecasts are already stale.

charts.desc: Charts inside — AutomationBench cost-per-task comparison across GPT-6 Sol/Luna, Claude Opus 5 and Fable 5.

items.title: A Model With No Decode Phase Answers 27 Questions in 0.114 Seconds for $0.00008
items.idea: TypeSafe's Jev model answers a full set of typed yes/no, multiple-choice and scoring questions in a single forward pass, with no token-by-token decoding — 27 questions, 0.114 seconds, $0.000081 total, while GPT-5.6 was still generating one text answer. Jev is trained with a method TypeSafe calls RLCD (reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions) so its output probabilities are honest: when it says 0.8, it's right about 80% of the time across many answers.
items.angle: If a meaningful share of enterprise LLM calls are actually classification, routing or scoring rather than open-ended generation, a chip built for one-pass judgment needs a completely different memory and compute profile than the HBM-heavy, decode-optimized accelerators the market has been building for.
items.tweetA: What happens to Groq and Cerebras if the fastest-growing slice of 'AI inference' turns out not to need decode at all? Jev answers 27 classification questions with calibrated probabilities in 0.114 seconds for $0.00008 — no token-by-token generation, no decode-bound bottleneck.
items.tweetB: Structured Outputs still generate token by token under constrained decoding — slow and expensive. Jev skips decode entirely for judgment calls: classify, route, score. If 'agents making decisions' turns out to be a bigger inference market than 'agents writing text,' the accelerator roadmap optimized for decode-bound workloads is solving the wrong problem for a real chunk of demand.

charts.desc: CHART WORTH SAVING — the head-to-head latency chart: Jev returns all 27 typed answers in 0.114s for $0.000081 while GPT-5.6 Terra is still generating its first answer token by token.

items.source: Robert Sinn, citing Tom Woolrych (Money of Mine)
items.title: A Geologist-PM Flags Snowline Gold as Still Sitting Without a Takeover Offer
items.idea: On Money of Mine, geologist-turned-fund-manager Tom Woolrych flagged specific junior gold names below where he thinks the market has repriced them: a conservative 5-6Moz read on San Lorenzo Gold's Salvadora deposit, Q2 Metals still under a $1B market cap despite its resource base, and Snowline Gold (TSX:SGD) sitting without a takeover offer despite being one of the more talked-about discovery stories in the sector.
items.angle: Junior gold M&A has lagged the metal's rally into record territory — these are the names a specialist thinks the market hasn't repriced yet as majors look for reserve replacement.
items.tweetA: A geologist-turned-PM says Snowline Gold ($SGD.TO) is still sitting without a takeover offer despite being one of the more talked-about discoveries in the space. Gold's near record highs, majors need reserve replacement, and the M&A wave in juniors hasn't caught up yet.
items.tweetB: Q2 Metals is still under a $1B market cap. With gold where it is and majors starved for ounces, that's the kind of gap specialists get paid to find before the M&A premium shows up in the price.

charts.desc: No charts — podcast summary; geological models were walked through visually on the episode itself, not in the newsletter text.

items.title: Silver Is Lagging Both of the Trades It's Supposed to Ride
items.idea: Tavi Costa flags silver's price lag versus copper as one of the market's most compelling current divergences — silver theoretically captures both copper's industrial-demand tailwind and gold's monetary-demand tailwind simultaneously, yet hasn't repriced to reflect either fully as the year-end setup builds.
items.angle: A dual-driver metal lagging both of its reference assets into year-end is a classic mispriced-optionality setup, though the specific ratio levels sit inside the paywalled 50-chart deck.
items.tweetA: Silver is supposed to get gold's monetary bid AND copper's industrial bid. Right now it's capturing neither — it's lagging both metals into year-end. That's not a story, that's a mispriced call option on two macro theses converging at once.
items.tweetB: Copper's at all-time highs on the AI/grid buildout. Gold's near records on de-dollarization flows. Silver sits at the intersection of both trades and hasn't moved. Is that a genuine lag about to close, or is silver telling you something neither of those other trades wants to hear?

charts.desc: 50 charts in the full paywalled report — the free preview shows only the intro; the silver/copper/gold ratio charts are inside.

items.title: 75% of Shares Are Held by Long-Term Investors — Most Earnings Calls Are Run for the Other 25%
items.idea: McKinsey's 2017 classic (recirculated with fresh data) finds roughly 75% of a company's shares are typically held by long-term, fundamentals-driven 'intrinsic investors,' not short-term traders. McKinsey's new 2026 Global Investor Survey found respondents care less about missing consensus estimates if the long-term strategy remains sound, and are increasingly using AI tools to analyze company disclosures directly rather than relying on management's framing.
items.angle: If investors are using AI to read filings themselves, the traditional 'manage the narrative on the earnings call' playbook loses power — sell-side narrative-shaping gets harder when the buy-side has an LLM reading the 10-K in parallel.
items.tweetA: 75% of shares in the average company are held by investors McKinsey calls 'intrinsic' — long-term, fundamentals-driven. Yet most management teams still run earnings calls to appease the loud short-term minority. The survey data says that's increasingly the wrong audience to optimize for.
items.tweetB: McKinsey's own 2026 survey: investors are increasingly using AI tools to analyze disclosures directly. If the buy-side has an LLM reading the 10-K before the earnings call even starts, the sell-side's job of quietly framing the narrative just got a lot harder to do.

charts.desc: No chart — classic essay reprint plus survey commentary.

items.title: McKinsey Projects Some Tech Investment Categories Could Grow More Than 12x in a Single Year
items.idea: McKinsey's Technology Trends Outlook 2026 flags at least five tech domains on pace to more than double investment from 2025 to 2026, led by agentic software development and space technologies — both projected to potentially grow more than 12x in a single year. AI infrastructure, AI for scientific discovery, and robotics also show substantial projected growth.
items.angle: A 12x investment multiple in a single year is bubble-adjacent by any definition — worth tracking whether that money is venture dollars, corporate capex, or both, since that determines who absorbs the drawdown if the agentic-coding or space-tech thesis slips even a year.
items.tweetA: McKinsey projects some tech categories — agentic software development, space tech — could grow more than 12x in a single year. That's not an adoption curve, that's a doubling-down bet. Worth asking who's writing those checks and what happens if the thesis takes even one more year than expected.
items.tweetB: 'More than 12x investment growth in one year' sounds like a chart you'd screenshot to call a top, not a bottom. McKinsey frames it as a trend to watch, not a warning — but a category compounding that fast usually means either a real phase change or a very short runway before the correction.
